prompt: What product forms when 4-octyne is hydrogenated with H2 over a palladium on carbon (Pd/C) catalyst?

choices.text: octane
cis-4-octene
choices.why: That is the Lindlar catalyst's product. Pd/C is more active and carries the reduction on to the alkane.

choices.text: trans-4-octene
choices.why: Trans alkenes come from sodium or lithium in liquid ammonia, not from catalytic hydrogenation.

choices.text: 4-octanol
choices.why: Hydrogenation adds only hydrogen. No oxygen is introduced.

explanation: Alkynes are reduced to alkanes by addition of H2 over a metal catalyst, in two steps through an alkene. With Pd/C, complete reduction occurs, so 4-octyne gives octane. The less active Lindlar catalyst stops at cis-4-octene.

prompt: How many moles of H2 are taken up when 1 mol of 4-octyne is completely reduced to octane over Pd/C?
explanation: The reduction occurs in two steps through an alkene. The first H2 converts 4-octyne to 4-octene, and the second converts 4-octene to octane, so 2 mol of H2 are used.

prompt: In the hydrogenation of an alkyne to an alkane, which step is more exothermic?

choices.text: The first step, alkyne to alkene
The second step, alkene to alkane
choices.why: Measurements show the opposite: the first step releases more heat.

choices.text: Both steps release exactly the same amount of heat
choices.why: The section says the first step is more exothermic than the second.

choices.text: Neither; both steps absorb heat
choices.why: Both steps are exothermic; the first is more so.

explanation: The reduction of an alkyne to an alkane occurs in two steps through an alkene intermediate, and measurements show that the first step (alkyne to alkene) is more exothermic than the second (alkene to alkane).

choices.text: Palladium on CaCO3, deactivated with lead acetate and quinoline
Palladium on carbon, made more active by adding quinoline
choices.why: Pd/C is the catalyst that reduces alkynes all the way to alkanes. The Lindlar catalyst is less active: lead acetate and quinoline deactivate it.

choices.text: Lithium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia at −33 °C
choices.why: That is the dissolving-metal reduction, which gives trans alkenes. The Lindlar catalyst is a palladium catalyst.

choices.text: Mercury(II) sulfate dissolved in aqueous sulfuric acid
choices.why: That is the catalyst for alkyne hydration, not hydrogenation.

explanation: The Lindlar catalyst is finely divided palladium metal precipitated onto a calcium carbonate support and then deactivated by treatment with lead acetate and quinoline, an aromatic amine. Because it is less active than Pd/C, hydrogenation stops at the alkene stage.

prompt: What product forms when 4-octyne reacts with 1 equivalent of H2 over the Lindlar catalyst?

choices.text: cis-4-octene
trans-4-octene
choices.why: The hydrogens add with syn stereochemistry, to the same side, so the alkene is cis. Trans alkenes come from Li in liquid NH3.

choices.text: octane
choices.why: Complete reduction happens with Pd/C. The less active Lindlar catalyst stops at the alkene.

choices.text: A 1:1 mixture of cis- and trans-4-octene
choices.why: Syn addition gives the cis alkene, not a mixture.

explanation: Lindlar hydrogenation stops at the alkene and occurs with syn stereochemistry (Section 8.5), giving a cis alkene. 4-Octyne gives cis-4-octene; further hydrogenation over Pd would give octane.

prompt: In the Hoffmann–LaRoche synthesis of vitamin A, Lindlar hydrogenation first gives the cis isomer. How is it converted into the trans isomer?

choices.text: By heating
By reducing it with Li in liquid NH3
choices.why: Li/NH3 reduces alkynes to trans alkenes. Here the double bond is already formed, and the cis isomer is converted by heating.

choices.text: By further hydrogenation over Pd/C
choices.why: That would reduce the double bond to a single bond rather than change its geometry.

choices.text: By treating it with lead acetate and quinoline
choices.why: Those are what deactivate the Lindlar catalyst. They don't convert cis to trans.

explanation: Hoffmann–LaRoche uses alkyne hydrogenation in its commercial synthesis of vitamin A. Hydrogenation over the Lindlar catalyst gives the cis isomer (7-cis-retinol), which is converted to the trans isomer by heating.

prompt: What product forms when 5-decyne is treated with lithium in liquid ammonia?

choices.text: trans-5-decene
cis-5-decene
choices.why: Cis alkenes come from Lindlar hydrogenation. Li/NH3 is complementary: it gives trans alkenes.

choices.text: decane
choices.why: This method converts an alkyne to an alkene; it doesn't continue to the alkane.

choices.text: A 1:1 mixture of cis- and trans-5-decene
choices.why: The trans vinylic anion forms and is protonated without equilibrating, so the product is the trans alkene.

explanation: Sodium or lithium metal in liquid ammonia reduces an alkyne to a trans alkene. This complements the Lindlar reduction, which gives cis alkenes. In the section's example, 5-decyne gives trans-5-decene in 78% yield.

prompt: In the section's example, what is the percent yield of trans-5-decene from 5-decyne and lithium in liquid ammonia?
explanation: 5-Decyne gives trans-5-decene in 78% yield on treatment with lithium in liquid ammonia.

prompt: At what temperature, in °C, do alkali metals dissolve in liquid ammonia to give the solution used for alkyne reduction?
explanation: Alkali metals dissolve in liquid ammonia at −33 °C to produce a deep blue solution containing the metal cation and ammonia-solvated electrons. The alkyne is then added to this solution.

prompt: In the Li/NH3 reduction, an electron first adds to the triple bond to give an anion radical. What is an anion radical?

choices.text: A species with a negative charge and an odd number of electrons
A neutral species with an odd number of electrons
choices.why: That is an ordinary radical. An anion radical also carries a negative charge.

choices.text: A negatively charged species with all its electrons paired
choices.why: That is an ordinary anion. An anion radical also has an odd number of electrons.

choices.text: A species with two negative charges and no unpaired electrons
choices.why: Only one electron has been added, so the species has one negative charge and an odd number of electrons.

explanation: An anion radical is both an anion (it has a negative charge) and a radical (it has an odd number of electrons). It forms when an electron adds to the triple bond, and it is a strong base, able to remove H^+ from ammonia.

prompt: Which sequence of intermediates matches the lithium/ammonia reduction of an alkyne?

choices.text: Anion radical → vinylic radical → vinylic anion → trans alkene
Vinylic radical → anion radical → vinylic anion → trans alkene
choices.why: The first event is addition of an electron, which gives the anion radical. Protonating it with NH3 then gives the vinylic radical.

choices.text: Anion radical → vinylic anion → vinylic radical → trans alkene
choices.why: After the anion radical is protonated, the vinylic radical gains the second electron to become a vinylic anion, not the other way round.

choices.text: Vinylic cation → vinylic radical → vinylic anion → trans alkene
choices.why: Vinylic cations appear in electrophilic additions. Li/NH3 adds electrons, so the first intermediate is an anion radical.

explanation: Figure 9.5.1: an electron adds to the triple bond to give an anion radical, which removes H^+ from ammonia to give a vinylic radical. A second electron gives a vinylic anion, which abstracts a second H^+ from ammonia to give the trans alkene.

prompt: How many electrons are added to each alkyne molecule during its reduction by lithium in liquid ammonia?
explanation: One electron adds to the triple bond to form the anion radical, and a second adds to the vinylic radical to form the vinylic anion. Each electron addition is followed by removal of H^+ from ammonia, so the alkyne gains two electrons and two protons.

prompt: Why does the Li/NH3 reduction give a trans alkene rather than a cis alkene?

choices.text: Vinylic radicals equilibrate quickly, but the less hindered trans vinylic anion forms and is protonated before it can equilibrate
Both hydrogens add to the same side of the triple bond at once
choices.why: That is syn addition, which is how Lindlar hydrogenation gives cis alkenes.

choices.text: The cis alkene forms first and is converted to trans by heating
choices.why: Heating is how the cis vitamin A isomer is converted. In Li/NH3 reduction the trans geometry is set when the vinylic anion forms.

choices.text: Vinylic anions equilibrate quickly, so the more stable trans anion builds up before protonation
choices.why: It is the other way round: vinylic radicals equilibrate rapidly, but vinylic anions equilibrate much less rapidly.

explanation: Trans stereochemistry is established in the second reduction step (step 3), when the less hindered trans vinylic anion is formed from the vinylic radical. Vinylic radicals undergo rapid cis–trans equilibration, but vinylic anions equilibrate much less rapidly, so the more stable trans anion is formed and then protonated without equilibration.

prompt: Using an alkyne, how would you prepare trans-2-octene?

choices.text: Reduce 2-octyne with Li in liquid NH3
Reduce 2-octyne with H2 over the Lindlar catalyst
choices.why: Lindlar hydrogenation is a syn addition and gives cis-2-octene.

choices.text: Reduce 2-octyne with H2 over Pd/C
choices.why: Pd/C carries the reduction all the way to octane.

choices.text: Reduce 3-octyne with Li in liquid NH3
choices.why: The double bond forms where the triple bond was, so 3-octyne would give trans-3-octene.

explanation: A trans alkene comes from the alkyne with its triple bond in the same position, reduced with lithium or sodium in liquid ammonia. 2-Octyne with Li/NH3 gives trans-2-octene (Exercise 9.5.1a).

prompt: Using an alkyne, how would you prepare cis-3-heptene?

choices.text: Reduce 3-heptyne with H2 over the Lindlar catalyst
Reduce 3-heptyne with Li in liquid NH3
choices.why: Li/NH3 gives the trans alkene, trans-3-heptene.

choices.text: Reduce 2-heptyne with H2 over the Lindlar catalyst
choices.why: The double bond forms where the triple bond was, so 2-heptyne would give cis-2-heptene.

choices.text: Reduce 3-heptyne with H2 over Pd/C
choices.why: Pd/C reduces the alkyne completely, to heptane.

explanation: Syn hydrogenation over the Lindlar catalyst gives a cis alkene and stops at the alkene stage. 3-Heptyne therefore gives cis-3-heptene (Exercise 9.5.1b).
